card: Paper card. Question: What are the optimization strategies of high-entropy alloys for electrocatalytic applications?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) composed of five or more equiatomic or near-equiatomic components. Processing: Various methods including carbon thermal shock, moving bed pyrolysis, magnetron sputtering, electrodeposition, and dealloying. Findings: HEAs have a highly disordered structure and a wide range of composition modulation, showing excellent performance in mechanical properties, magnetic properties, and electrocatalysis; HEAs have abundant active sites, high selectivity, and high stability, making them ideal catalytic materials in electrocatalytic reactions; The high entropy effect, slow diffusion effect, lattice distortion effect, and cocktail effect of HEAs contribute to their unique properties and performance; Element regulation, defect regulation, and strain engineering are effective strategies for optimizing HEA catalysts. Mechanism: The high entropy effect, slow diffusion effect, lattice distortion effect, and cocktail effect of HEAs contribute to their unique properties and performance. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of HEAs in electrocatalytic applications and to develop more efficient synthesis methods and optimization strategies. Quote: "High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are expected to become one of the most promising functional materials in the field of electrocatalysis"

Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be optimized for electrocatalytic applications?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with various compositions, such as CrMnFeCoNi, CuMnFeCoNi, and MnFeCoNi. Findings: 1.0; 2.0; 3.0; HEAs have shown potential in electrocatalytic research due to their excellent combined properties; The introduction of Cu causes the original ORR performance to deteriorate, while the introduction of Cr improves the original catalytic performance; The randomly distributed metal elements promote the formation of a large number of active centers on the surface of HEAs. Mechanism: The inherent surface complexity of HEAs can provide nearly continuous adsorption energy and increase the proportion of active sites. Limitations: There are still many challenges in the research of the catalytic mechanism and practical applications. Future work: The combination of theory and experiment is very important to understand the catalytic mechanisms of HEAs. Quote: "HEAs have shown more and more obvious potential in electrocatalytic research due to their excellent combined properties"

card: Paper card. Question: How can a quinary refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) be designed to exhibit high thermal stability and superior resistance to extreme irradiation environments (specifically heavy ion irradiation and helium implantation) without precipitation or grain coarsening?. System: Quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA; specific compositions: W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 (thin film) and W31Ta34Cr5.0V27Hf3.0 (thick film). Processing: Magnetron-sputtering deposition from metal targets (99.99% purity) at room temperature, 3 mTorr pressure, and no bias voltage; thin films (100 nm) on NaCl substrates and thick films (3 µm) on W substrates; in situ TEM annealing at 1173 K for 10 minutes; ex situ irradiation at 1073 K.. Test conditions: In situ TEM ion irradiation at 1173 K using 1-MeV Kr+2 and 16 keV He+ (dual-beam) to 8.5 dpa and ~9% He; single-beam 16 keV He+ implantation to ~9%; ex situ 400 keV Ar+2 irradiation to 10 dpa at 1073 K; nanoindentation at 200 nm depth; APT analysis.. Findings: Average grain size of as-deposited sample was 24.5 ± 1.3 nm, increasing to 26.3 ± 1.1 nm after annealing at 1173 K.; Grain refinement occurred during dual-beam irradiation, with average grain size dropping to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after ~94 mins.; No dislocation loops were detected even after 8.5 dpa and 9.13% He implantation during dual-beam experiments.; Cavity formation saturated after 5 dpa, with total volume change of ~0.3% after 8.45 dpa and higher He percentages.; Unirradiated sample hardness was 13.25 GPa, increasing to 16.25 GPa after annealing and 20 GPa after irradiation.; Hf segregates to grain boundaries after annealing but depletes from grain boundaries during irradiation.; No precipitation was observed in irradiated samples, unlike the quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA which showed Cr-V precipitation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the high irradiation resistance to a combination of factors: high density of stable grain boundaries causing grain refinement via cascade effects (where cascades larger than grain size break grains), chemical complexity altering defect recombination rates, and a decrease in the order-disorder transition temperature (ODTT) which promotes homogenization and prevents precipitation. The absence of dislocation loops is linked to high interstitial-vacancy recombination and a rough energy landscape for He migration that favors smaller, uniform bubble nucleation.. Limitations: The authors acknowledge that the study used ion irradiation rather than neutron irradiation, stating that 'further work (e.g., response to neutron irradiation) is necessary to advance the technology readiness level (TRL) of this material'. They also note that different compositions can have different SRO parameters and segregation behaviors, and that tensile measurements on coarse grain and bulk forms are needed.. Future work: The authors propose that 'tensile measurements should follow on coarse grain and bulk forms' and that 'the effect of SRO on the mechanical behavior of future RHEA in extreme environments is another research topic to be further explored'. They also suggest the design methodology can be used to 'devise and synthesize new RHEAs for different applications'.. Quote: "Grain refinement occurred, and the average grain size dropped to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after a total irradiation time of ~94 mins."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a high-entropy alloy be designed to simultaneously achieve high yield strength and high crack-initiation fracture toughness, overcoming the typical trade-off between these properties?. System: Al0.5CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy (composition: Cr ~22.5%, Co ~24.6%, Fe ~23.2%, Ni ~24.5%, Al ~5.21 wt%). Processing: Laser powder-bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing using an Nd:YAG fiber laser (300 W power, 50 µm layer thickness, 90 µm hatch spacing, 500 mm.s−1 scanning speed) followed by optional heat treatments (e.g., 750 °C for 1 h). Test conditions: Tensile tests at 298 K and 77 K with strain rate 10−3 s−1; Fracture toughness tests (C(T) specimens) at 298 K and 77 K using J-integral-based R-curves. Findings: Yield strength (σy) of as-printed alloy is ~729 ± 31 MPa at 298 K and ~942 ± 11 MPa at 77 K.; Crack-initiation fracture toughness (KJIc) is ~306 MPa√m at 298 K and ~290 MPa√m at 77 K.; The as-printed alloy shows ~47% higher KJIc than wrought CrCoNi at 298 K.; The as-printed alloy shows ~66% higher yield strength than wrought CrCoNi at 298 K.; Heat treatment (HT3: 750 °C, 1 h) increases yield strength to ~1090 MPa at 298 K but reduces KJIc to ~135 MPa√m.; At 77 K, the heat-treated alloy exhibits unstable crack growth with KJIc dropping to ~51 MPa√m.; Dislocation bands spread up to ~300 µm away from the crack tip in the as-printed honeycomb microstructure.; Nano-twinning is activated at 77 K in the as-printed alloy, with twin growth restricted by B2 phase boundaries.. Mechanism: The nano-bridged honeycomb microstructure provides strength via the ordered B2 phase and high dislocation density, while the dislocation nano-bridges connecting the B2 phase on cell boundaries act as highways for dislocation movement away from the crack tip, facilitating crack blunting and shielding to enhance intrinsic toughness.. Limitations: Conventional heat treatments that form uniformly distributed B2 precipitates restrict dislocation movement away from the crack tip, leading to a significant reduction in fracture toughness (e.g., ~5.7 times lower at 77 K compared to the as-printed state).. Future work: Manipulating the thermal gradient (G) and solidification rate (R) during 3D printing to alter the size of the honeycomb cells and tailor the material's strength and fracture toughness for specific applications.. Quote: "The dislocation nano-bridge form in the regions of the cell boundaries where solutes (Al/Ni) concentration was insufficient to the form B2 phase."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the surface mechanical properties and wear behavior of SS410 steel be enhanced through the reinforcement of gas-atomized AlCrCoFeNi High Entropy Alloy (HEA) particles using Friction Stir Processing (FSP), and what are the optimal process parameters for minimizing wear rate?. System: AlCrCoFeNi equimolar High Entropy Alloy (HEA) powder reinforced on SS410 stainless steel substrate. Processing: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) using a pinless tool to compact powder in a trapezoidal groove (4 mm depth, 3:1 width ratio) followed by a tungsten carbide tapered pin tool (16 mm shoulder diameter, 4.5 mm length, 4 mm pin diameter); parameters: 900 rpm rotational speed, 20 mm/min traverse speed, 10 kN applied load. Test conditions: Microhardness (100 gf load, 15 s dwell); Tensile testing (transverse direction); Wear testing (Pin-on-disc tribometer) with applied load (10–50 N), sliding distance (500–2500 m), and sliding velocity (0.5–2.5 m/s). Findings: Microhardness increased by 41.3% to 482 HV at the center of the Stir Zone (SZ).; Ultimate tensile strength increased by 39.1% to 832 MPa compared to the FSP-base metal.; Mean grain size in the SZ was refined to 2.84 μm (range 0.347 μm–8.5 μm).; High Angle Grain Boundaries (HAGB) fraction reached 49.7%.; The regression model for wear rate prediction showed R² = 95.41% and adjusted R² = 94.89%.; Confirmation tests showed an error percentile within ±4% between predicted and experimental wear rates.; Applied load was identified as the most influential factor on wear rate, followed by sliding velocity and sliding distance.; The wear rate decreased with increasing sliding velocity due to protective oxide layer formation.. Mechanism: Enhancement is attributed to grain refinement via discontinuous Dynamic Recrystallization (DRX) and Severe Plastic Deformation (SPD), the Hall-Petch relationship, Particle Stimulated Nucleation (PSN) mechanism, Zener pinning (barrier effect) hindering grain growth and dislocation movement, and the load-bearing capacity of HEA particles. The formation of an oxide layer at higher sliding velocities also protects the surface against adhesive wear.. Limitations: Surface modification is limited to a few extensions; the process is ineffective for soft and brittle materials; and the FSP tool design significantly influences grain refinements.. Future work: Application of HEA-reinforced FSP samples in the fabrication of surgical equipment, aircraft bearings, and the repair/maintenance of boilers and storage tanks in nuclear and chemical industries.. Quote: "The microhardness and ultimate tensile strength of the FSP-HEA sample are increased by 41.3 % and 39.1 % respectively due to the high degree of refined grains with 2.84 μm and evenly distributed HEA particles."

card: Paper card. Question: How does ultrafine-grain microstructure affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy. Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) at 400 and 1800 rpm for 5 min. Test conditions: Oxidation at 850-1050 °C for 100 h in laboratory air. Findings: Ultrafine-grain microstructure reduces oxidation kinetics by 12-48%; Parabolic rate constant is lower for ultrafine-grained samples; Activation energy for oxidation is higher for ultrafine-grained samples; Protective oxide scales of Al2O3 and Cr2O3 form on ultrafine-grained samples; Internal oxidation zone (IOZ) forms in ultrafine-grained samples. Mechanism: The enhanced oxidation resistance of ultrafine-grained samples is attributed to the formation of a dense protective Cr2O3 layer followed by internal Al-rich oxide layered structure, which acts as a barrier for the oxidation process. card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of CoCrCuFeTi High Entropy Alloy (HEA) as a reinforcement through Friction Stir Processing (FSP) affect the tribological behavior of Stainless Steel (SS304)?. System: CoCrCuFeTi High Entropy Alloy (HEA) reinforced SS304. Processing: Friction Stir Processing (FSP) with a tungsten carbide tool rotating at 1000 rpm, traverse speed of 25 mm/min, and a load of 10 kN, followed by annealing at 650 °C for 2 h. Test conditions: Pin-on-disc wear test with varying load (10-40N), sliding velocity (0.5–3.5 m/s), and sliding distance (500–2000 m). Findings: The processed sample with HEA after annealing offered 29.8%, 57.4%, and 58.49% improved wear resistance at the minimum level of load, sliding velocity, and sliding distance than the processed base samples; The worn surface morphology revealed delamination, abrasion, adhesion, and oxide layer formation as the predominant wear mechanisms; The addition of HEA particles induced dislocation and hindered grain growth, leading to improved microhardness and wear resistance. Mechanism: The authors propose that the improved wear resistance is due to the synergistic effect of the ultrafine refined grains by the FSP process and the stress relieved microstructures after annealing, as well as the dislocation-strengthening mechanism involved in the process. Quote: "The processed samples exhibited excellent refinement in grains with uniform HEA reinforcement distribution"

card: Paper card. Question: How does copper content affect the microstructure, wear, and corrosion resistance of CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloys manufactured by powder metallurgy?. System: CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloys with copper content varying from 0 to 20 at. %. Processing: Powder metallurgy methods: mechanical alloying and hot pressing of element mixtures, with parameters such as rotational speed of jars (694 rpm), duration (30 min), grinding bodies-to-powder weight ratio (15:1), temperature (950 °C), pressure (35 MPa), and isobaric exposure (3 min). Test conditions: Tribological tests with a high-precision tribometer, corrosion resistance tests in 3.5% NaCl solution. Findings: The solubility limit of copper in CoCrFeNi solid solution is 9 at. %; Doping with copper increases wear resistance by 23% due to solid solution hardening; Wear resistance declines with increasing copper concentration due to segregation of the excess FCC2 phase and decreasing hardness; The wear products are amorphous particles consisting of the alloy components with uniformly distributed oxygen and silicon elements; Formation of the duplex structure FCC1 + FCC2 has a beneficial effect on corrosion resistance compared to the single-phase HEA; Corrosion current density decreases monotonically from 2.24 to 0.4 mA·cm−2 as copper concentration increases from 10 to 20 at. %. Mechanism: The increase in wear resistance is attributed to solid solution hardening caused by distortion of the crystal lattice of the (Fe)Co,Ni,Cr solid solution, while the decline in wear resistance is due to segregation of the excess FCC2 phase and decreasing hardness. Quote: "The solubility limit of copper in CoCrFeNi solid solution was found to be 9 at. %"

card: Paper card. Question: Can a rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe be synthesized and what are its properties?. System: (Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O. Processing: bottom-up method using oxalate precursors, annealed at 1000°C for 6 hours in argon with MnO2 as an oxygen generator. Test conditions: various temperatures and atmospheres, including air, argon, and 5% H2/Ar. Findings: FeO-HEO has a single-phase rocksalt structure; cation site occupancy is highly random; metal ions are unanimously divalent; improved structural robustness compared to constituent binary oxides; antiferromagnetic order with a magnetic transition temperature of ~218 K. Mechanism: the oxygen sublattice acts as a buffer layer to accommodate different metal ions, and the cocktail effect contributes to the improved phase stability. Future work: dedicated study to determine the magnetic structure and correlations, and assessment of whether iron carries an orbital magnetic moment in this FeO-HEO. Quote: "a generic method was developed to synthesize rocksalt high-entropy oxides containing divalent manganese and iron"

card: Paper card. Question: Can machine learning models predict the phases of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with high accuracy?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with 50 different elements. Findings: XGBoost and Random Forest models achieved 97% accuracy in predicting solid solution phases; XGBoost model achieved 86% accuracy in predicting all 11 phase categories; The inclusion of IM phases had a more pronounced impact on accuracy compared to the inclusion of AM phases; Mixing enthalpy and VEC are important features for predicting phase stability in HEAs; Atomic radius is a effective descriptor for distinguishing between BCC and AM phases. Mechanism: The authors propose that the machine learning models can learn the complex relationships between the features and the phases of HEAs, allowing for accurate predictions. Limitations: The dataset is imbalanced, with some phase categories having more records than others. Future work: The authors suggest that future work should focus on exploring the use of other machine learning models and features to improve the accuracy of phase predictions. Quote: "XGBoost and Random Forest consistently outperform the other models, achieving 86% accuracy in predicting all phases"

Paper card. System: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) with varying compositions, including FCC, BCC, BCC+FCC, IM, BCC+IM, FCC+IM, BCC+IM, BCC+FCC+IM, AM, BCC+AM, FCC+AM, and BCC+FCC+AM phases. Findings: 1. The BCC structure is the most frequently mentioned in the literature, closely followed by the FCC structure.; 2. The dual-phase structure combining both FCC and BCC is also commonly discussed.; 3. The majority (93%) of the data falls within the range of four to six components.; 4. The alloys in the dataset consist of 50 different elements.; 5. Certain elements, including Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, Al, Cu, Ti, Mn, V, Zr, Mo, Nb, Ta, and Zn, are more commonly used in the fabrication of HEAs.; 6. The Adaptive Synthetic Sampling approach was used to generate synthetic data and mitigate class imbalance issues.; 7. The ExtraTreesClassifier algorithm was employed for feature selection, resulting in 12 features suitable for HEAs phase classification.. Quote: "The dataset utilized in this paper was sourced from various references,,,, encompassing 11 different categories and comprising a total of 11,252 records of HEAs."

card: Paper card. Question: How to systematically document experimentally reported high-entropy alloy microstructures and metallurgy-specific features to support machine learning-based phase classification?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 1362 multicomponent alloys selected through the end of August 2020, excluding glassy, amorphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases. Processing: Synthesis routes, hot- or cold-working, homogenization (temperature and time), annealing (temperature and time), and quenching were extracted from peer-reviewed experimental articles. Test conditions: Data derived from experimental peer-reviewed research articles; no new experimental testing was performed in this data article. Findings: The dataset contains 1422 entries with seventeen columns covering identification, composition, empirical parameters, processing, and microstructure; The final dataset includes 1362 multicomponent alloys after removing entries with missing data and eliminating glassy, amorphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases; Microstructural phases are categorized as single solid solution (FCC, BCC), dual-phase (FCC+BCC), or other intermetallic/laves/martensitic phases (Im); Empirical design parameters calculated include density estimate, enthalpy of mixing (dHmix), entropy of mixing (dSmix), melting temperature (Tm), valence electron concentration (VEC), atomic size difference (δ), and difference in Pauling negativities (χ); Visualization shows that solid solution phases are particularly more sensitive to empirical parameters than intermetallic (IM) phases. Mechanism: The authors explain that the dataset serves as a systematic documentation to enable machine learning and material informatics methods to extract insights and trends not immediately available from individual studies. Limitations: The article is limited to typical empirical parameters for succinctness, though others can be developed from alloy specifications. Future work: Different machine learning and material informatics computational methods can be applied to this dataset to extract insights and trends thereby advancing the real-world applications of these alloys. Quote: "After removing entries missing some data and eliminating glassy, amourphous, and hexagonal close-packed phases, the as-constructed dataset is reduced to 1362 multicomponent alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: Can machine learning reliably predict the crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC, MIP) of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) synthesized via melting and casting routes without using synthetic data augmentation, and is synthetic data augmentation a reliable practice for this domain?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 30 elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mn, Ti, V, Nb, Mo, Zr, Hf, Ta, W, C, Mg, Zn, Si, Re, N, Li, Sn, Be, B, Ag, Pt, Y, Pd, Au); specifically a novel alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25.. Processing: Vacuum arc melting of elemental buttons (Ni, Cu, Fe, Co, Al; purity > 99.99%) under high purity Ar environment, followed by multiple melting/solidification cycles for homogeneity, vacuum sealing in quartz tube, homogenization at 1000 °C for 10 h, and water quenching.. Test conditions: Machine learning models trained on 1200 experimental datasets from melting/casting routes; tested on 240 samples from original data and 279 samples from augmented data (1200 original + 192 synthetic); XRD analysis performed with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) at 20°–100° (2θ).. Findings: The vanilla Random Forest Classifier (V-RFC) achieved the highest performance with an average test accuracy of 84%, ROC-AUC score of 0.9649, and tenfold cross-validation mean score of 0.9315.; Synthetic data augmentation using SMOTE-Tomek links increased average test accuracy to 92% (1392 datasets) but did not yield significant breakthroughs in correct/incorrect phase predictions compared to the original dataset.; The V-RFC model correctly predicted the FCC phase for the newly synthesized alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25, which was confirmed by XRD showing Bragg's peaks (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222).; Five physical parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) were identified as crucial for phase prediction, with no strong multicollinearity observed between them.; The model was limited in interpreting the exact number and types of phases in complex multiphase HEAs, often classifying them broadly as MIP (Mixture of Intermetallic Phases).; Hyper-parameter tuning of the RFC model (HT-RFC) resulted in an approximate 3% increment in average test accuracy to 87.49%.; The study found that mixing data from different synthesis routes causes spurious effects, justifying the exclusion of non-melting/casting routes from the dataset.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the Random Forest Classifier's ensemble of decision trees effectively handles the imbalanced dataset of experimental data without the need for synthetic augmentation, which they claim introduces uncertainty regarding whether generated samples are truly high-entropy alloys. The model relies on the correlation of five thermodynamic and geometric parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) to distinguish between solid-solution phases (FCC, BCC) and intermetallic mixtures (MIP).. Limitations: The method is limited in exactly interpreting the number and types of phases present in a complex multiphase HEA, as it typically predicts such cases as a single 'MIP' category rather than resolving specific phase combinations.. Future work: A follow-on work will test and predict the mechanical properties of HEAs, which will require atomistic studies using Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with EAM potentials for 16 elements (Cu, Ag, Au, Ni, Pd, Pt, Al, Pb, Fe, Mo, Ta, W, Mg, Co, Ti, Zr).. Quote: "We found that (i) RFC model predictions were more reliable in contrast to other models and (ii) the synthetic data augmentation is not a neat practice in materials science specially to develop HEAs, where it cannot assure phase information reliably."

card: Paper card. Question: How does thermomechanical processing (TMP) tune the microstructure and room-temperature tensile properties of a Co-rich Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) TRIP-HEA?. System: Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) high-entropy alloy. Processing: High-frequency induction melting and casting; forging at 1473 K; solution treatment at 1473 K for 4 h followed by water quenching (AS); hot-rolling at 1473 K to 50% reduction (HR); warm-rolling at 973 K to 50% reduction (WR); cold-rolling at 293 K to 50% reduction followed by heat treatment at 973 K for 30 min (HT1) or 1023 K for 30 min (HT2). Test conditions: Room temperature (293 K) tensile tests at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; Vickers hardness measurement with 500 g load for 15 s. Findings: Grain size was refined from 144.4 μm in the as-solutionized (AS) sample to 1.83 μm in the HT1 sample.; Yield strength increased from 254.6 MPa (AS) to 641.3 MPa (HT2), and ultimate tensile strength increased from 702.5 MPa (AS) to 968.4 MPa (HT2).; Tensile elongation of the HT2 sample retained a satisfactory value of 68.8% despite the significant strength increase.; Nanosized Cr-rich σ-phase precipitates formed in HT samples with a volume fraction of 0.413% (HT1) and 0.681% (HT2).; The average size of precipitates was 118.8 nm for HT1 and 89 nm for HT2.; Precipitation strengthening contribution (Δσp) was estimated at 10.5 MPa for HT1 and 17.9 MPa for HT2.; Grain boundary strengthening contribution (Δσg) was calculated as 323.9 MPa for HT1 and 247.6 MPa for HT2.; The WR sample exhibited the lowest strain-hardening rate, which decreased rapidly with increasing strain.. Mechanism: Grain refinement is the primary mechanism for enhancing strength while retaining ductility, whereas nanosized incoherent precipitates provide a dual effect: they refine grains via Smith–Zener drag and block dislocation motion via Orowan strengthening, though they slightly sacrifice ductility.. Limitations: The formation of incoherent precipitates inevitably sacrifices ductility, which needs to be considered for optimizing TMPs.. Future work: The authors state that the results provide guidelines for fabricating high-performance materials and insights into the regulation of microstructure and mechanical properties of TRIP-HEAs, but do not explicitly list specific future experiments.. Quote: "The results showed that grain refinement is an effective strategy for enhancing strength while retaining satisfactory ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the hot deformation behaviors, dynamic recrystallization mechanisms, and grain refinement capabilities of the Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 TRIP-HEA under varying temperatures and strain rates?. System: Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at.%) TRIP-HEA. Processing: Hot compression of cylindrical samples (12 mm height × 8 mm diameter) to a true strain of 1.0 (63% reduction) at temperatures of 1123, 1173, 1223, and 1273 K with strain rates of 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 s−1; samples were heated to 1473 K, held for 300 s, cooled to compression temperature, held for 10 s, compressed, and water quenched.. Test conditions: Compression temperatures: 1123–1273 K; Strain rates: 0.1–0.001 s−1; True strain: 1.0; Zener–Hollomon parameter (Z) varied by temperature and strain rate.. Findings: The apparent activation energy for hot deformation was measured to be 385.7 kJ/mol.; The peak flow stress increased with an increase in strain rate and/or a decrease in temperature.; The volume fraction of dynamically recrystallized (DRX) grains ranged from 4.8% (at 1123 K, 0.1 s−1) to 82% (at 1273 K, 0.001 s−1).; The average diameter of DRXed grains ranged from 5 to 20 μm across all investigated conditions.; Discontinuous dynamic recrystallization (dDRX) was predominant at small Zener–Hollomon parameters (high temperature, low strain rate), while continuous dynamic recrystallization (cDRX) prevailed at large Z values.; A necklacelike structure composed of fine equiaxed grains and coarse elongated grains formed at medium Z values.; The constitutive equation showed a linear correlation between ln(sinh(ασ)) and lnZ with a fitting coefficient of 0.994.; Homogeneous grain structures with a size of approximately 19 μm were achieved at 1273 K and 0.001 s−1.. Mechanism: The flow softening is driven by dynamic recrystallization (both dDRX and cDRX) which consumes stored dislocation energy. dDRX nucleates at grain boundaries via bulging, favored by high temperature and low strain rates due to high grain boundary mobility. cDRX occurs via subgrain formation and rotation, favored by high strain rates and low temperatures where dislocation recovery is impeded. The high activation energy (385.7 kJ/mol) indicates sluggish diffusion, which hinders dynamic recovery and grain growth, leading to higher peak stresses and finer grain sizes compared to conventional alloys.. Limitations: The study notes that grain growth often occurs at elevated temperatures to minimize grain boundary energy, which can counteract refinement efforts at very high temperatures and low strain rates.. Future work: The study provides guidelines for optimizing grain morphology and mechanical properties of the TRIP-HEA through thermomechanical processing such as hot-compression, hot-rolling, and hot-extrusion.. Quote: "The apparent activation energy was estimated to be ~385.7 kJ/mol."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of 0.71 wt.% Zr affect the microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion resistance of a CoCrFeMoNi high-entropy alloy designed for geothermal applications?. System: CoCrFeMoNi (Sample 1) and CoCrFeMoNi + 0.71 wt.% Zr (Sample 2). Processing: Vacuum arc remelting (VAR) using MRF ABJ 900 VAR equipment under argon atmosphere with six remelting operations for homogenization; samples ground and polished to mirror finish with 0.1 µm alumina suspension. Test conditions: Three-point bending test (ISO 7438:2020) for Young's modulus; microhardness test (1.96 N load, ISO 14577-1:2015); electrochemical tests in 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature including linear polarization (±25 mV vs Ecorr, 0.166 mV/s sweep), potentiodynamic polarization (-1.2 to +1.2 V vs SCE), and EIS (10⁻¹ to 10⁵ Hz). Findings: The Young's modulus of the Zr-free alloy (Sample 1) was 20.5% higher than that of the Zr-doped alloy (Sample 2).; The addition of Zr increased the average microhardness of the high-entropy alloy.; The corrosion rate increased from 2.44 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 1 to 2.80 × 10⁻³ mmpy for Sample 2, representing a ~16-fold increase compared to Sample 1.; The polarization resistance (R2) of the passive film decreased from 2.57 × 10⁷ kΩ·cm² for Sample 1 to 1.47 × 10⁵ kΩ·cm² for Sample 2.; The addition of Zr caused grain refinement and reduced the volume fraction of interdendritic zones.; The tendency to form the sigma phase was diminished in Sample 2 due to a decrease in Mo concentration in interdendritic zones from 20 at.% to 17 at.%.; Both alloys exhibited brittle fracture with cleavage-like fracture planes.. Mechanism: The decrease in corrosion resistance and passive film resistance with Zr addition is attributed to the formation of a thicker but more defective passive film containing an increased number of defective spots, potentially involving the in situ formation of ZrO2 which explains the high corrosion rate. The grain refinement and hardness increase are due to Zr obstructing grain coarsening and creating a supersaturated solid solution.. Limitations: The volume fraction of ZrO2 was below the detection limit of XRD, preventing direct phase identification of the oxide despite TEM evidence in other studies.. Quote: "The addition of Zr resulted in a decrease in the value of the Young modulus but also in a decrease in corrosion resistance."

W2883475578.title: Enhanced strength and ductility of a tungsten-doped CoCrNi medium-entropy alloy

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying the nickel atomic ratio (x = 1.0, 1.4, 1.8) in the AlCrFeCoNi system affect the microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in simulated body fluids?. System: AlCrFeCoNix alloys with x = 1.0, 1.4, and 1.8. Processing: Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR) using high purity raw materials (≥99.5%), followed by flipping and re-melting 6 times under Argon; homogenization via annealing at 1100 °C for 48 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Immersion in Ringer Grifols solution at 37 ± 0.1 °C for one week; potentiodynamic polarization from -800 mV to +500 mV vs SCE at 1 mV/s; Vickers microhardness with 100 g load for 15 s. Findings: Hardness values decreased from 562 HV for AlCrFeCoNi to 455 HV for AlCrFeCoNi1.4 and 316 HV for AlCrFeCoNi1.8.; The pitting potential (Enp) increased with nickel content: 185 mV for x=1.0, 245 mV for x=1.4, and 385 mV for x=1.8.; Al concentration in the surface region dropped from ~10 at% to 2.57–3.03 at% after heat treatment and corrosion.; Open circuit potential increased by 30–50 mV during the first 24 hours due to passive layer growth.; The extent of interdendritic areas increased with nickel concentration, with Cr more segregated in interdendritic areas than in dendrites.; Corrosion current densities were much lower than those of 304SS, indicating higher resistance to general corrosion.. Mechanism: The decrease in hardness is attributed to the dissolution of Cr and Fe precipitates in the nickel-rich matrix, forming a continuous solid solution. The improved corrosion resistance with higher Ni content is linked to a more positive pit nucleation potential and a larger difference between nucleation and repassivation potentials, suggesting a strong tendency for pit repassivation. The formation of an Al-Ni compound after thermal treatment is hypothesized to corrode faster than the main HEA phase, leading to the observed drop in Al and Ni concentrations on the surface.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that Ni content is not the only factor affecting corrosion, as microstructure and element distribution also play roles.. Future work: The authors propose that by manipulating the composition and structure of HEAs, their mechanical and chemical performance could be optimized to meet the requirements for their usage as novel medical instruments materials.. Quote: "Hardness values decreased as the percentage of nickel increased due to the dissolution of the precipitates in a nickel-rich matrix and consequently the formation of continuous solid solutions."

W2967481309.title: Design and in-situ characterization of a strong and ductile co-rich multicomponent alloy with transformation induced plasticity

card: Paper card. Question: What are the thermal stability, phase transition temperatures, and microstructural evolution of the metastable intermetallic phases in the CoCrFeMo0.85Ni high-entropy alloy?. System: CoCrFeMo0.85Ni high-entropy alloy (gas atomized powder, nominal equimolar CoCrFeNi with 0.85 Mo). Processing: Gas atomization of high-purity Co, Cr, Fe, Mo, and Ni powders (approx. 24 µm); thermal analysis via DTA and DSC with 5 K/min heating/cooling cycles up to 1400 °C under Ar atmosphere; interrupted DTA at 900 °C; microstructural characterization via FEGSEM, EDX, and EBSD. Test conditions: Heating and cooling cycles at 5 K/min up to 1400 °C; interrupted heating at 900 °C; analysis of as-received powder, interrupted sample, and fully solidified sample. Findings: Solidus and liquidus temperatures determined as 1323 °C and 1331 °C, respectively.; Phase transitions observed at 800 °C (exothermal formation of intermetallics) and 1212 °C (endothermic dissolution).; As-received powder exhibits fine alternating layers suggesting spinodal-like morphology with minor elemental segregation.; After full thermal cycles, a dendritic microstructure forms with a single-phase FCC matrix.; The FCC matrix is depleted in Mo (<1/3 of dendrite content) and enriched in Ni compared to the dendrite core.; Dendrite cores contain a tetragonal (Co, Cr, Fe)-rich phase (presumed σ) surrounded by a Mo-rich rhombohedral phase (presumed µ).; The precipitation window for the cooling curve is identified between 780 °C and 1200 °C.; CALPHAD predictions show a single FCC phase above 1280 °C, which disagrees with DTA-derived liquidus at 1331 °C.. Mechanism: The formation of the FCC matrix is driven by high mixing entropy reducing Gibbs free energy. During solidification, Mo partitions to the liquid phase due to its high melting point and sluggish diffusion, segregating to interdendritic regions. The metastable phases (σ and µ) form via spinodal decomposition and compositional modulation driven by segregation, where Mo enrichment acts as a precursor state. The coexistence of σ and µ phases is attributed to cooperative diffusion and the order of elemental partitioning, with the µ phase growing at the periphery of the σ phase.. Limitations: The CALPHAD method may require further assessment for the transition temperatures of intermetallic formation in this HEA. The stabilization of the σ phase is a gradual process that is too slow to be fully observed in the DTA experiments due to kinetic effects. The study notes that the interaction of metastable phases in powder form can be eliminated by high-temperature treatment, limiting the observation of certain short-term phenomena.. Future work: Further detailed thermal analysis should be performed to derive remaining thermodynamic properties such as partial pressure and activity. Additional investigation of intermetallic phases is needed to facilitate understanding of atomic arrangement and orientation for optimal HEA design.. Quote: "Solidus and liquidus temperatures of CoCrFeMo0.85Ni were determined by differential thermal analysis as 1323 °C and 1331 °C, respectively."
